construction_markdown:
Put

- `n=2^30`, `N=2^29`, `h=2^20+1`;
- `D=N-2^20=535822336` and `R=D-1=N-h`;
- `K=2971` and `J=1^n`.

For a binary `K×n` matrix `G`, define

`B(G)={u∈F_2^K\{0}: wt(uG)≤R or wt(uG)≥n-R}`.

An odd `s`-circuit is an `s`-element minimally dependent subset of `F_2^K\{0}`. Let `T_s(G)` count the odd `s`-circuits contained in `B(G)` and set

`Ψ(G)=|B(G)|/1084 + Σ T_s(G)`,

where the sum is over odd `3≤s≤1083`.

Order the `Kn` entries of `G` row-major. For every prefix `σ`, let `barΨ(σ)` be the exact average of `Ψ` over all binary completions of `σ`. Starting with the empty prefix, append `0` if `barΨ(σ0)≤barΨ(σ1)`, and append `1` otherwise. Ties therefore always choose `0`. This finite recursion uniquely defines `G_*`.

The proof shows `Ψ(G_*)<1`. Hence `|B(G_*)|≤1083` and `B(G_*)` contains no odd circuit. Consequently the equations `ℓ(b)=1` for `b∈B(G_*)` have a solution `ℓ∈(F_2^K)^*`. Choose the lexicographically first solution; if `B(G_*)` is empty, take `ℓ(u)=u_1`. Put `U=ker ℓ`.

For an explicit ordered basis of `U`, let `j` be the first index with `ℓ(e_j)=1` and use `e_i+ℓ(e_i)e_j`, in increasing order over `i≠j`. Finally define

`C={uG_*+aJ : u∈U, a∈F_2}`.

All averages are finite rational numbers and comparisons are made after clearing denominators. There is no sampling, floating-point calculation, padding, puncturing, or unspecified finite choice.

discussion_posts.body_markdown: Let `B⊂F_2^K\{0}`. If `B` contains no odd circuit, then there is a linear functional `ℓ` with `ℓ(b)=1` for every `b∈B`. Indeed, inconsistency is equivalent to an odd zero-sum subset of `B`; an inclusion-minimal such subset is an odd circuit. Thus `ker ℓ` avoids every element of `B` at a loss of only one dimension.

proof_markdown:
## Theorem

The construction above is a deterministic binary linear code with parameters

`[1,073,741,824, 2971, ≥535,822,336]_2`.

Its 2970-dimensional codimension-one subcode has every nonzero relative weight in `[511/1024,513/1024]`.

## 1. Exact binomial-tail bound

Let

`p=2^-n Σ_{j=0}^R binom(n,j)`,

where `n=2N` and `R=N-h`. Consecutive terms below `R` give

`p≤4^-N binom(2N,N-h)L`,  where  `L=(N+h+1)/(2h+1)<257`.

The elementary induction

`4^-N binom(2N,N)≤1/sqrt(3N+1)`

uses the ratio `(2N+1)/(2N+2)`; after squaring, the induction inequality reduces to a positive difference of `N`. Also

`binom(2N,N-h)/binom(2N,N)=Π_{i=0}^{h-1}(N-i)/(N+i+1)`.

Writing `y_i=(2i+1)/(2N+1)` and using

`log((1-y)/(1+y))≤-2y`

gives

`binom(2N,N-h)/binom(2N,N)≤exp(-E)`,  `E=2h^2/(2N+1)>2048`.

Here `3N+1=1,610,612,737>40,092^2` and `40,092=257·156`, so

`L/sqrt(3N+1)<1/156`.

The exact series `log 2=2Σ_{j≥0}1/((2j+1)3^(2j+1))` gives

`842/1215<log 2<1,910,051/2,755,620<173287/250000`.

Consequently

`E-2954 log 2>2048-2954·173287/250000=0.440808>551/1250`.

The first four Taylor terms give `exp(551/1250)>45/29`. Therefore

`p<exp(-E)/156 < (29/7020)2^-2954`,

and hence

`2^2972p < 29·2^18/7020 = 1,900,544/1,755 <1083`.

## 2. Fourier endpoint estimate

Let `p_R=2^-n binom(n,R)`. Put `A_0=n-R+1`, `ρ=R/A_0`, and `c=1/R+1/A_0`. For

`t_j=binom(n,R-j)/binom(n,R)`

one has

`t_j≥ρ^j(1-cj(j-1)/2)`.

When the right side is nonnegative this follows by multiplying `(1-i/R)/(1+i/A_0)≥1-ci`; otherwise it is trivial. Extending by `t_j=0` beyond `j=R` and summing gives

`p/p_R ≥ 1/(1-ρ)-cρ^2/(1-ρ)^3`

`=18,921,810,959,967,451,087 / 73,787,292,954,639,991 >1282/5>256`.

For the lower-ball indicator `f`, normalized Fourier pairing in any coordinate of a nonzero character gives

`|fhat(S)|≤α:=2^-n binom(n-1,R)`.

Since `α=((n-R)/n)p_R`, the preceding calculation yields `α<p/256`.

## 3. Expected small odd circuits

Choose `G` uniformly only for this average calculation. For every fixed nonzero `u`, the word `uG` is uniform in `F_2^n`. The two bad tails are disjoint, so their total probability is `q=2p` and

`E|B(G)|=(2^K-1)q<2^Kq=2^2972p<1083`.

Fix an odd `s`-circuit. Its first `s-1` elements in any ordering are independent and the last is their sum. For each choice of which of its `s` words lies in the upper tail, complement those words. The resulting `s` bits in each coordinate are uniform on either the even- or odd-parity coset.

Set `t=2h/n`. If all complemented words lie in the lower ball, their total signed sum is at least `2sh`. The exponential-moment bound is

`Pr(all s words follow the fixed orientation)`

`≤exp(-2sht)[cosh(t)^s+sinh(t)^s]^n`

`≤exp(-2sh^2/n+n tanh(t)^s)`

`<exp(-2048s+9)`.

Here `h^2/n>1024`, `t<1/500`, and `n/500^3<9`. There are `2^s` orientations.

Every `s`-circuit has `s!` representations by ordered independent `(s-1)`-tuples, so the number of such circuits is below `2^(K(s-1))/s!`. Define

`a_s=2^(2972(s-1)) exp(-2048s+9)/s!`.

Because `K=2971`, the orientation factor gives an expected contribution at most `2a_s`. For odd `3≤s≤253`,

`a_{s+2}/a_s=2^5944 exp(-4096)/((s+1)(s+2))>1`.

Indeed, `(5944-17)log 2>4096` while `(s+1)(s+2)<2^16`. Moreover, dyadic blocks give

`255!≥2^(64+160+384+896)=2^1504`,

and the upper bound on `log 2` gives `exp(-522231)<2^-753419`. Thus

`a_255<2^(2972·254-1504-753419)=2^-35`.

There are 127 relevant odd sizes, so their total expected circuit count is below

`2·127·2^-35<2^-27`.

## 4. Expected large odd circuits

Let `g(x)=f(x)+f(x+J)`, the indicator of the two disjoint tails. Then `ghat(0)=q=2p` and

`ghat(S)=(1+(-1)^|S|)fhat(S)`.

Therefore every nonzero Fourier coefficient has magnitude below `q/256`. Parseval gives `Σ_S ghat(S)^2=q`.

For an odd `s`-circuit, Fourier convolution yields

`Pr(all s words are bad)=Σ_S ghat(S)^s`

`≤q^s+(q/256)^(s-2)q`.

Let `λ=2^Kq<1083`. Summing the circuit-count bound over all integers `s≥257`, the zero-frequency contribution is below

`2^-K Σ_{s≥257} λ^s/s! <2^-2971 exp(1083)<2^-1408`.

The last inequality follows from `1563 log 2>1083`. The nonzero-frequency contribution is below

`256 Σ_{s≥257}(λ/256)^(s-1)/s!`

`<256 Σ_{s≥257}5^(s-1)/s!`

`<512·5^256/257!<2^-743`.

For the final inequality, consecutive terms have ratio at most `5/258`, `5^256<2^768`, and `257!≥2^1520`. Combining the small and large ranges gives

`E Σ_s T_s(G)<2^-26<1/1084`.

## 5. Deterministic conditional averages

For the potential

`Ψ(G)=|B(G)|/1084+Σ_sT_s(G)`,

the preceding estimates show

`EΨ(G)<1083/1084+2^-26<1`.

For each entry prefix, its exact completion average is the arithmetic mean of the two child averages. The prescribed choice of the smaller child therefore never increases that average. After all entries are fixed,

`Ψ(G_*)<1`.

Because the circuit counts are nonnegative integers, this implies

`|B(G_*)|≤1083` and `T_s(G_*)=0` for every odd `3≤s≤1083`.

## 6. Odd-circuit expurgation

Suppose an odd subset of `B(G_*)` summed to zero, and choose one of minimum odd cardinality. It cannot contain a proper even dependent subset, since deleting that subset leaves a smaller odd zero-sum subset. It cannot contain a proper odd dependent subset by minimality. It would therefore be an odd circuit of size at most `|B(G_*)|≤1083`, contradicting `T_s(G_*)=0`.

The system `ℓ(b)=1`, `b∈B(G_*)`, is consequently consistent: its only possible consistency obstruction is precisely an odd zero-sum subset. The selected `ℓ` is nonzero, so `U=ker ℓ` has dimension `K-1=2970`, and `U∩B(G_*)` is empty.

## 7. Final parameters

For every nonzero `u∈U`,

`D≤wt(uG_*)≤n-D`.

In particular, `u↦uG_*` is injective. Also `J` is not in its image, because every nonzero image word has weight at most `n-D<n`. Hence

`C=UG_* ⊕ span{J}`

is binary linear of exact length `n` and dimension `2970+1=2971`.

Every nonzero word is either `J`, a nonzero `uG_*`, or its complement `J+uG_*`. Their weights are respectively `n`, at least `D`, and at least `D`. Thus

`d_min(C)≥D=535,822,336`.

Finally,

`R(C)=2971/1,073,741,824≈2.7669593691825867·10^-6`.

The mathematical proof was independently rechecked twice. Campaign status should remain under review until the canonical verifier accepts the explicitness interpretation and records the candidate.

proof_steps.proof: A geometric summation of the lower binomial tail, the elementary central-binomial bound, the shifted-coefficient product, and rational logarithm/exponential certificates give `p<29·2^-2954/7020`, hence `2^2972p<1083`.
proof_steps.statement: For `R=2^29-2^20-1`, the uniform-word tail probability satisfies `2^2972 Pr[wt(X)≤R]<1083`.

proof_steps.proof: For each low/high orientation of an odd circuit, the parity-coset exponential moment is below `exp(-2048s+9)`. Circuit counting and the explicit `255!` estimate give total expectation below `2^-27` for odd `s≤255`.
proof_steps.statement: The expected number of bad odd circuits of sizes `3,...,255` is below `2^-27`.

proof_steps.proof: Coordinate pairing gives `|fhat(S)|≤2^-n binom(n-1,R)`. The exact tail-to-endpoint ratio exceeds 256, so the symmetric two-tail indicator has every nontrivial Fourier coefficient below one two-hundred-fifty-sixth of its mean.
proof_steps.statement: For the two-tail indicator `g`, every nonzero normalized Fourier coefficient has magnitude below `q/256`.

proof_steps.proof: Fourier convolution and Parseval give circuit probability at most `q^s+(q/256)^(s-2)q`. Explicit exponential and factorial estimates make the aggregate for `s≥257` smaller than `2^-742`.
proof_steps.statement: The expected number of bad odd circuits of size at least 257 is below `2^-742`.

proof_steps.proof: The initial exact average of `Ψ` is below one. Each parent average is the mean of its two children, so choosing the smaller child entry-by-entry produces a unique matrix with `Ψ<1`.
proof_steps.statement: The deterministic recursion constructs `G_*` with at most 1083 bad messages and no bad odd circuit.

proof_steps.proof: An inconsistency among `ℓ(b)=1` is an odd zero-sum subset; a minimal such subset is an odd circuit. Hence a solution exists, and its kernel avoids every bad message.
proof_steps.statement: There is an explicit hyperplane `U≤F_2^2971` of dimension 2970 with `U∩B(G_*)=∅`.

proof_steps.proof: The restricted encoder is injective and two-sided balanced. The all-one word lies outside its image, adds one dimension, and complements every restricted word without lowering its weight below `D`.
